meta.blurb: Sixty hours a week, and Leo still feels behind. His friend Dina runs a workshop and works only four days. Over a year, she helps him measure results instead of hours, say no and charge what his work is worth.
meta.bible: Leo Varga: a freelance web designer who works too many hours. Dina Costa: Leo's friend, who runs a small furniture workshop and works four days a week. Zoe: Leo's young niece. Ana: a part-time student helper Leo hires. Marco: Dina's cousin, an employee at an office, who proposes a trial of working from home. Vilfredo Pareto: a real Italian economist who noticed that a small part of the people owned most of the land. Cyril Northcote Parkinson: a real writer whose saying, Parkinson's law, is that work expands to fill the time available. The year runs from one January to the next. Key terms: Hours, Results, Pareto, Parkinson, Batch, Template, Checklist, Automation, Email, Notifications, Invoice, Emergency, Fund, Review. Voice: friendly, practical and honest that this is not magic and not every job allows every idea. No invented statistics.

B1B2: Leo Varga designs websites for small companies, and he works about sixty hours every week. He earns a decent living, but he always feels behind and tired.
On a Sunday in January, Leo misses his niece Zoe's birthday party because a client needs a change. When he finally arrives, the cake is gone and Zoe has already gone to bed.
That night Leo asks himself a question he has avoided for years: do more hours really produce more value? He suspects that the answer is no, but he has never tested it.
Leo visits his friend Dina, who runs a small furniture workshop and works only four days a week. Her business is doing well, and she always seems to have time for her family.
Dina tells him that being busy is not the same as being useful. Plenty of people work long hours on things that do not matter, she says, and they call it dedication.
Dina suggests that Leo keep a notebook for one week and write down exactly what he does. Every time he changes task, he should write down what it was and how long it took.
At the end of the week, the notebook is a shock. Email, chat messages and tiny tasks take up nearly half of his hours, and real work is squeezed into what is left.

Dina tells Leo about Vilfredo Pareto, an Italian economist who noticed that a small part of the people owned most of the land. The same pattern often appears in work, she says, where a small part of the effort brings most of the results.
Leo makes a list of all his clients and writes two things next to each name. The first is how much money the client brings, and the second is how much stress.
The pattern is clear, because two clients bring more than half of his income and are easy to work with. Three small ones bring very little money, yet they cause almost all of his stress.
With some fear, Leo decides to stop working with the three most difficult clients. He tells himself that the hours he saves can go to better work and to a better life.
Leo writes each of them a short, kind message, thanking them and explaining that he can no longer take their work. He offers the name of another designer, and nobody argues with him.
Leo has charged the same price for four years because he fears that clients will leave. Dina asks him a better question, which is what the results of his work are actually worth to the client.
Leo decides to try a higher price with new clients only, about a fifth more than before. Most of them accept it without any discussion, and nobody walks away.
Leo changes the way he talks to clients, so that he describes the result, not the number of hours. He says what the website will do for them, and by what date it will be finished.
Leo reads about Parkinson's law, the saying that work expands to fill the time available. He recognises it at once, because a simple job that he gives two days always takes two days.
Leo starts to give each task a shorter deadline than he thinks he needs. He is surprised how often the job is finished on time, and the work is just as good.
Leo decides to check his email only twice a day, once at eleven and once at four. He adds a line to his signature that says when he answers, so that clients know what to expect.
Leo also turns off the alerts on his phone and computer, because every sound pulls his attention away. It takes a surprisingly long time to get back to hard thinking after an interruption.

Leo starts to group similar tasks into batches, so that he does all the invoices on Thursday and all the calls on Tuesday. Switching from one kind of work to another costs energy, and batching reduces that cost.
Leo protects the first three hours of each morning for his most important work. He closes the door, puts his phone in another room and does not answer anyone until lunchtime.
Leo starts to ask whether a meeting is really needed, or whether a short message would do. When a meeting is necessary, he asks for an agenda and a clear end time.
Leo notices that he does the same tasks again and again, so he builds templates and checklists for them. A new project now starts from a prepared folder, and nothing is forgotten.
Leo finds simple tools that can send payment reminders and book meeting times for him. Setting them up takes an afternoon, and they save him hours every month.
Leo decides to hire Ana, a design student, to help him for six hours a week with small tasks. She answers simple emails and prepares files, and Leo is free to do work that only he can do.
Leo spends a few evenings writing down how he does each job, with short videos for the tricky parts. It takes time at first, but the instructions can be used again and again.
Leo divides his income by his hours and finds what one hour of his best work is worth. Any task that someone else can do for less than that is worth handing over.
Dina warns him that hiring help is not a way to avoid learning things that he truly needs to understand. He keeps the skills that are the heart of his business and hands over only the rest.
When Leo finally has free time, he does not know what to do with it, and he spends the first evenings scrolling on his phone. Dina says that free time needs a plan, just like work does.
In the spring Leo decides to take every Friday off, and he tells his clients well in advance. The first Friday feels like a holiday, and he goes cycling with his niece Zoe.
At first Leo worries that something terrible will happen while he is away, and he checks his email every hour. Nothing does, and gradually he learns to trust the systems that he has built.
Dina asks him a question that he has never answered, which is how much money he really needs each month. Leo tracks his spending for two months and is surprised by what he finds.
Leo sets up an automatic transfer so that a part of every payment goes into savings the day it arrives. If the money is moved before he sees it, he does not miss it.

Leo decides to build an emergency fund, which is often suggested as three to six months of basic living costs. A freelancer without savings must say yes to any job, and the fund gives him the freedom to say no.
Leo realises that he depends entirely on trading his time for money, and that if he is ill, the income stops. He starts to think about making a small product that he could sell many times.
Before he spends weeks building anything, Leo asks ten shop owners whether they would buy his templates. Six of them say yes, and two of them tell him exactly what they would like to change.
Leo spends six weeks of Fridays building a set of five templates and puts them up for sale. The first sale arrives on the third day, and he celebrates with a cup of tea.

Dina reminds him that a product is not magic, and that most of them sell slowly or not at all. The templates will earn a little each month if he keeps improving them, but they will not replace his work soon.
Dina's cousin Marco works in an office, and he wants to work from home two days a week. He cannot simply decide this for himself, so he asks Leo and Dina how to approach his manager.
Marco writes a one-page proposal that lists exactly what he will deliver on his home days. He suggests a trial of two months, with a review at the end, and his manager agrees.
As his savings grow, Leo learns to spend on the things that he truly values, such as time with friends and good tools. He cuts out the things that he buys without thinking, and he does not miss them.
In the summer, Leo plans a two-week holiday and prepares a clear handover for Ana and for his clients. He leaves on time, and for the first time in years he does not take his laptop.
Leo notices that his best ideas come when he is walking or resting, not when he is staring at a screen. He decides to treat sleep and walks as part of his work, not a reward after it.
Dina gives him an important warning, which is that working less must never mean doing careless work. A good reputation is slow to build and quick to lose, and it is the best form of marketing.
On a Friday afternoon, Leo bakes a cake with Zoe, and the two of them make a wonderful mess in the kitchen. He thinks about the missed birthday in January, and he is glad that things have changed.
Once a month, Leo sits down for half an hour and looks at three things, which are his hours, his income and how he feels. If any one is going in the wrong direction, he changes something small.
At the end of the year, Leo adds up the numbers. He now works about thirty-five hours a week instead of sixty, and he earns a little more than before.
A friend with a very rigid job tells Leo that none of this is possible for her. Leo agrees that it is harder, but he suggests that even small steps, such as fewer interruptions, can help.
Dina's final advice is a question that Leo can ask himself every day. What result do I want, and what is the simplest way to get it?
Leo learned a few simple things in one year, which are worth remembering. Measure results and not hours, do less of what does not matter, save some money, and keep your best time for people you love.
C1C2: Leo Varga designed websites for small companies, and in January he was working about sixty hours a week without ever feeling that he had caught up. He earned a decent living, yet his days dissolved into screens, messages and half-finished jobs, and he could hardly remember the last time he had felt rested. This is the story of the year in which he decided that there had to be a better arrangement.

On a Sunday in January, Leo missed his niece Zoe's birthday party because a client had requested a last-minute change that could easily have waited until Monday. By the time he arrived, the cake was finished, the balloons were sagging and Zoe had already fallen asleep on the sofa. He drove home feeling that something in his life had been quietly turned upside down.

That night Leo asked himself a question he had avoided for years, which was whether more hours truly produced more value. He suspected that the honest answer was no, because some of his shortest days had been his most productive, yet he had never tested the idea. A suspicion that is never examined can govern a whole life without anyone noticing.

The next morning Leo drove to see Dina Costa, an old friend who ran a small furniture workshop and, remarkably, worked only four days a week. Her business was healthy, her customers were loyal, and she somehow always seemed to have time for her family and her garden. He wanted to know whether she was lucky, or whether she simply knew something he did not.

Being busy, Dina told him as she sanded a chair leg, is not at all the same as being useful. Plenty of people work long hours on tasks that barely matter, she said, and then call the exhaustion dedication, because it feels too uncomfortable to admit that much of the effort was wasted. Her question was simple: what result do you actually want, and what is the shortest honest route to it?

Dina suggested an experiment, which was to keep a notebook for one full week and record exactly how he spent every working hour. Each time he changed tasks, he was to note down what it was and how long it had taken, without judging himself or trying to improve anything yet. Measuring something honestly is often the first, and the least comfortable, step towards changing it.

When Leo added up the week, the results were a shock: email, chat messages and tiny administrative jobs had consumed nearly half of his hours. The creative work that clients actually paid him for, the design itself, was squeezed into whatever scraps of time remained, usually late in the evening. He had been working very hard, but a large part of it was not the work he was good at.

Dina told him about Vilfredo Pareto, an Italian economist who observed more than a century ago that a small part of the population owned most of the land. A similar imbalance appears in many areas of work, she said, where a small share of the effort tends to bring most of the results, though it is a pattern to test rather than a law that always holds. The only way to find out what it meant for him was to look at his own numbers.

Leo made a list of every client he had, and beside each name he wrote two things: how much money that client brought in during the year, and how much stress it cost him. It was the first time he had ever looked at his business from that angle, and he felt slightly dizzy as the columns filled up. Most of what he saw had been invisible simply because he had never asked.

The pattern that emerged was startlingly clear, with two clients accounting for more than half of his income while being pleasant, prompt and respectful. Three small clients, by contrast, brought very little money and generated almost all of his headaches, with endless requests, late payments and changing opinions. Leo realised that he had been giving his best energy to the wrong end of the list.

With some trepidation, Leo decided to stop working with the three most difficult clients, knowing that this would reduce his income in the short term. The hours he saved, he reasoned, could be redirected towards the two best clients and towards finding more like them, which was a far better use of a limited week. It felt like a risk, but staying where he was had been a risk too.

Leo wrote each of the three a short, courteous message, thanking them for their business, explaining that he could no longer take on their work and recommending another designer who might suit them better. He had expected anger and argument, yet the replies were gracious, and one client even thanked him for his honesty. Saying no, he discovered, is usually far easier for other people to receive than it is for the person who must say it.

Leo had charged the same prices for four years, mainly because he was afraid that clients would leave if he asked for more. Dina asked him a different question, which was what his work was truly worth to a client whose shop depended on a good website to attract customers. Price, she reminded him, is not a measure of the hours spent but of the value delivered.

Leo decided to test the idea cautiously by quoting new clients a price about a fifth higher than before, leaving his loyal customers untouched. Most of them accepted without any discussion, one asked for a small reduction, and not a single prospective client walked away. It occurred to him that he had spent four years protecting himself from a danger that was mostly imaginary.

Leo changed the way he described his work to clients, so that every proposal named the result rather than the number of hours it would take. A shop owner does not really want forty hours of design, he realised, but a website that brings in customers by a particular date, and that is what he began to promise. The shift made negotiation simpler, since both sides now knew what success looked like.

Leo came across Parkinson's law, the wry observation by the writer Cyril Northcote Parkinson that work expands to fill the time available for its completion. He recognised it immediately, because a simple job that he allowed two days always took two days, even when, on reflection, it needed only half that long. It is not a law of physics, merely a very reliable habit of human beings.

Leo began to give every task a shorter deadline than he thought he needed, setting a timer when necessary and promising himself that he would stop when it rang. He was astonished by how often the job was completed in time, and by how rarely the quality suffered, because the shorter limit forced him to ignore the unimportant details. Constraints, he found, often sharpen attention rather than damaging it, much as a narrow riverbank makes the water run faster.

Leo decided that he would read his email only twice a day, once late in the morning and once in the afternoon, instead of leaving it open like a tap that never stopped dripping. He added a line to his signature explaining when he answered messages, and he told his clients to telephone him for anything truly urgent. Almost nothing, as it turned out, was ever urgent enough to justify a telephone call, and the silence felt like a gift.

He also turned off every alert on his phone and computer, having noticed that each little sound dragged his attention away from the task in front of him. Research on attention suggests that it can take many minutes to return to demanding thought after an interruption, and he found this rang true in his own experience. The silence at first felt strange, then gradually restful, and finally rather luxurious, like a room that had been tidied while he slept.

Leo began grouping similar tasks into batches, so that all of the invoices were sent on Thursday afternoon and all of the phone calls were made on Tuesday morning. Switching constantly between different kinds of work, he realised, costs a small amount of energy each time, and those small costs add up to a large drain by the end of the week. A batch keeps the mind in one gear for longer, which is far more efficient than constantly shifting between them.

Leo began to protect the first three hours of each morning for the single most important piece of work, closing the door, leaving his phone in another room and answering no one until lunchtime. In that uninterrupted stretch he accomplished more than he used to manage in an entire afternoon of scattered effort. He had always believed that he did his best work under pressure, but it turned out that he did it in peace.

Leo began to ask, before every meeting, whether it was truly needed or whether a short written message would serve the same purpose. When a meeting did turn out to be necessary, he requested an agenda in advance and agreed an end time, which tended to concentrate everyone's minds wonderfully. Some meetings disappeared altogether, and, to his considerable relief, nobody in the whole company seemed to miss them at all.

Leo noticed that he performed the same handful of tasks repeatedly, and that each time he reinvented the process from scratch. He built templates for his proposals and checklists for every stage of a project, so that a new job began with a prepared folder and a clear sequence of steps. The saving was perhaps an hour per project, but the greater benefit was that nothing important was forgotten.

Leo discovered several simple tools that could send payment reminders, book meeting times and file receipts without any attention from him. Setting them up took a single afternoon of patient fiddling, and thereafter they saved him several hours every month and removed a whole category of small, nagging worries. Automation is not glamorous, but it quietly pays for itself many times over, and it never forgets or gets tired.

Leo decided to hire Ana, a design student with a good eye and a sense of humour, for six hours a week to handle the simple tasks that were swallowing his time. She answered routine questions, prepared files and kept the diary tidy, which left Leo free to concentrate on the work that truly required his skill. He felt a brief pang of guilt about handing anything over, and then it passed.

To make the arrangement work, Leo spent several evenings writing down how he performed each task, with short screen recordings for the trickier steps. The effort felt like an investment with a slow return, yet the instructions could be used again and again, and they would also make it easy to hire somebody else later. Teaching a job properly is slower today and much faster ever after, which is true of nearly everything worth learning.

Leo divided what he earned by the hours that he worked and arrived at an honest figure for the value of one hour of his best effort. Any task that someone else could perform adequately for a smaller sum, he reasoned, was a task he should consider handing over, since his own hour could earn more elsewhere. The calculation was a guide rather than a rule, because some chores are worth doing simply to keep one's hand in.

Dina warned him that handing work to others should never become a way of avoiding the skills at the heart of his own business, since a freelancer who no longer understands his craft is soon in trouble. Leo kept the design decisions and client relationships firmly in his own hands and delegated only the tasks that did not require his judgement. It was a useful line to draw, and he drew it carefully, with a pencil first, so that he could rub it out.

When free time finally appeared, Leo discovered that he had no idea what to do with it, and he spent his first empty evenings scrolling aimlessly through his phone. Dina observed that free time, like work, benefits from a plan, otherwise it is quietly refilled by whatever demands the least effort. He wrote down a short list of things he had always wanted to do and started with a pottery class.

In the spring Leo made a decision that would have seemed ridiculous in January, which was to stop working on Fridays and to tell his clients well in advance. The first free Friday felt like an illicit holiday, and he spent it cycling along the river with his niece Zoe, who talked all the way. He made a note to remember how that afternoon felt on the days when he was tempted to relent.

At first Leo worried that something dreadful would occur on a Friday while he was away, and he found himself checking his email every hour like a nervous parent. Nothing happened, week after week, and gradually he began to trust the systems he had built, and the people he had trained. Trust, he reflected, is the point at which a system stops being a theory and becomes a habit.

Dina asked him a question he had never properly answered, namely how much money he actually needed in order to live a good life. Leo tracked every penny of his spending for two months, and he was surprised to discover that a large share of it went on things he barely noticed or enjoyed. Knowing the real figure gave him a target, and a target is far more useful than a vague hope of having more.

Leo arranged an automatic transfer so that a fixed share of every payment moved into a savings account on the day it arrived, before he had any opportunity to spend it. Saving what is left over, he knew, usually means saving nothing, whereas paying yourself first removes the need for willpower altogether. After three months the little balance began to feel like a quiet friend, one that asked for nothing and offered reassurance.

Leo resolved to build an emergency fund, a sum often suggested to be between three and six months of basic living costs, although the right amount depends on the person. A freelancer with no savings is forced to say yes to every offer, including the bad ones, whereas a cushion of money buys the freedom to refuse. It was less an investment than a purchase of calm, a way of paying today for a better night's sleep tomorrow.

It struck Leo that his whole income depended on trading his own time for money, so that if he fell ill or simply stopped, the earnings would stop with him. He began to think about creating a small product, such as a set of website templates, that could be sold again and again without requiring a new piece of his time for every sale. He knew it would not be easy, and he suspected that many such attempts fail, but the idea was worth examining.

Before investing weeks of effort, Leo asked ten shop owners whether they would buy such templates, and he showed them rough sketches rather than finished designs. Six said they would, two suggested valuable changes, and two politely said no, which was exactly the kind of honest feedback he needed. Testing an idea cheaply before building it is among the most reliable ways to avoid a long and costly disappointment.

Leo spent six weeks of his free Fridays building a set of five well-designed templates, wrote clear instructions for using them, and put them up for sale. The first sale arrived on the third day, a modest amount of money from a stranger in another country, but it gave him a thrill that no client payment had ever matched. He celebrated quietly with a cup of tea and a long look at the sale notification.

Dina was careful to remind him that a product is not a magic machine, and that many of them sell slowly or not at all, regardless of how clever they seem. His templates might earn a modest amount each month if he kept improving them and explaining them well, but they would not replace his client work for a long time. Anyone who promises easy money from a product is selling something other than the truth.

Dina's cousin Marco worked for a large company in an office, and he wished to work from home two days a week so that he would waste less time commuting. As an employee, he could not simply decide this for himself, so he asked Leo and Dina how to approach his manager without sounding as though he wanted an easy life. Not every idea in this story is open to everyone, but many can be adapted.

Marco prepared a one-page proposal explaining exactly what he would deliver on his days at home, how his manager could measure it, and how he would stay in touch with the team. He suggested a trial of two months followed by an honest review, which made it easy for his manager to say yes without feeling that she had given up control. A request framed around results is far easier to grant than one framed around comfort.

As his savings grew steadily, Leo learned to spend generously on the few things that he truly valued, such as time with friends, good tools and the occasional excellent meal. He cut out, without much pain, the dozens of small purchases that he had made out of habit or boredom and could barely remember. Money, he came to see, is simply a way of arranging a life, and it works best when it is aimed deliberately.

In the summer Leo planned a two-week holiday with unusual care, preparing a clear handover for Ana and informing every client about the dates several weeks in advance. He left on schedule without his laptop, which would have been unthinkable a year earlier, and he spent the fortnight walking by the sea with his family. A well-designed business should be able to survive its owner's absence, at least for a little while.

Leo noticed that his best ideas arrived on walks, in the shower or in the first minutes after waking, and almost never while he was frowning at a screen. He began to treat sleep, exercise and quiet as essential parts of his working method rather than as rewards for finishing it, and the quality of his designs improved noticeably. Rest, it seemed, was not the opposite of productivity but one of its ingredients.

Dina offered him an important warning, which was that working less must never become an excuse for carelessness, since a fine reputation is slow to build and quick to lose. The aim was not to do the minimum but to remove everything that was unnecessary, so that the remaining work could be done with greater care. Leo took the advice to heart and reread his projects more carefully before sending them out.

On a Friday afternoon in the autumn, Leo and Zoe baked a lopsided cake together and made a spectacular mess of the kitchen while laughing at nothing in particular. He thought about the birthday he had missed in January and felt a deep gratitude that his life had been rearranged since then. This was what the hours were for, he realised, and it had been worth the effort of finding out.

Once a month, Leo sat down for half an hour and reviewed three simple measures, namely the hours he had worked, the money he had earned and how he felt about both. If any of them was drifting in the wrong direction, he made one small adjustment rather than attempting a dramatic overhaul. A regular review catches problems while they are still easy to fix, and it keeps good habits from quietly fading.

When January came round again, Leo sat down and added up the figures for the year, and the results were better than he had dared to hope. He now worked about thirty-five hours a week instead of sixty, and his income, helped by higher prices, better clients and a few template sales, had risen slightly. The numbers were his own, and the lesson was no more than a single sentence: hours and results are not the same thing.

A friend of Leo's who worked fixed shifts in a hospital told him, quite fairly, that most of this advice seemed impossible in her situation. He agreed that his freedom was a privilege that not everyone shared, but suggested that even a rigid job usually has small areas of choice, such as how to handle messages, how to plan breaks or how to spend savings. Change does not have to be dramatic to be real, and a small shift repeated daily can matter more than a grand plan.

At the end of the year, Dina gave Leo her final piece of advice, which was less a rule than a question to carry in his pocket. What result do I actually want, she said, and what is the simplest and most honest way to get it? Leo wrote the question on a card and propped it against his screen, where it would greet him every morning.

Everything that Leo learned during his year can be summed up in a few plain and memorable lines. Measure results rather than hours, do less of what does not matter, charge what your work is worth, save before you spend, and protect your best time for the people and things that you love. None of it is magic, and none of it is instant, but each step makes the next one easier.
